data.text:
chalmers johnson. CIA analyst turned dissident scholar. 2000 book titled blowback. the term itself comes from agency tradecraft: unintended consequences of covert operations the public never knew about, coming back decades later in forms nobody can connect to the original cause.

johnson's argument across 300 pages: the cost of america's global military presence keeps showing up on local ledgers, not just the federal budget. host nations absorb second-order effects of bases, training operations, deployments, intelligence partnerships. those effects rarely make it into the cost-benefit conversation between governments. they show up as protest, electoral pushback, surprise enemies, sometimes decades later.

US-japan relationship was johnson's primary case. okinawa bases, helicopter accidents, anti-base movements that took 30 years to mature into the political force they became in the 2000s. he predicted similar arcs for korea, the philippines, central asia. the cycle is: operate now, pay later, deny the connection when the bill arrives.

korea sits 70+ years into that cycle and most of it remains unpriced. THAAD deployment effects on chinese economic retaliation. defense procurement obligations that distort budgets. semiconductor controls that fragment supply chains. host-nation-support cost share that increases every renewal. each item alone reads as alliance maintenance. cumulatively they're the unpaid invoice johnson described.

the iran story matters here because it's the next blowback event in real time. saudi's base refusal is blowback for 40 years of US policy choices. iran's $100B insistence is blowback for 1953. korean banks at the table for $7B is blowback for cooperative oil settlement decisions from 2010. nothing happens in a vacuum and most invoices arrive late.

‘NO’ TO WPS HARASSMENT

Members of theFilipinos Do Not Yield (FDNY) Movement  and allied groups stage a lightning protest in front of the Chinese Embassy along Sen. Gil Puyat Avenue in Makati City on May 11 to condemn the continued harassment and aggressive presence of Chinese ships in the West Philippine Sea. 

📸: Norman Cruz
